Existing semi-supervised methods demonstrate substantial performance degra- dation compared to fully supervised approaches, particularly in small target segmentation and boundary refine- ment tasks. To address these fundamental challenges, we propose SASNet (Scale-aware Adaptive Supervised Net- work), a dual-branch architecture that leverages both low-level and high-level feature representations through novel scale-aware adaptive reweight mechanisms. Our approach introduces three key methodological innova- tions, including the Scale-aware Adaptive Reweight strategy that dynamically weights pixel-wise predictions using temporal confidence accumulation, the View Variance Enhancement mechanism employing 3D Fourier domain transformations to simulate annotation variability, and segmentation-regression consistency learning through signed distance map algorithms for enhanced boundary precision. These innovations collectively ad- dress the core limitations of existing semi-supervised approaches by integrating spatial, temporal, and geometric consistency principles within a unified optimization framework. Comprehensive evaluation across LA, Pancreas- CT, and BraTS datasets demonstrates that SASNet achieves superior performance with limited labeled data, surpassing state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods while approaching fully supervised performance levels. JSON: Name: sasnet_pipeline Title: Scale-aware adaptive reweighting with dual-branch multi-scale decoders and frequency-domain view-variance for semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation Short Hypothesis: For 3D medical image segmentation with ≤20% labeled volumes, combining a dual-branch decoder architecture (separate low-level and high-level decoders) with temporal confidence–weighted pixel-wise ensemble (Scale-Aware Adaptive Reweight), frequency-domain view-variance augmentation, and signed-distance-map–based segmentation–regression consistency yields higher mean Dice and lower HD95 than current state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods under identical training conditions. Related Work: Current semi-supervised medical segmentation approaches fall into three main families: self-training with pseudo-labeling, consistency-regularization (including Mean Teacher variants), and multi-scale feature fusion. Self-training improves utilization of unlabeled data but is vulnerable to noisy pseudo-label propagation and often uses ad-hoc confidence masking. Consistency-based methods enforce prediction stability under spatial augmentations or interpolation but typically use instantaneous uncertainty estimates and global weighting that can under- or over-emphasize unreliable voxels. Multi-scale strategies improve detection of small structures but are commonly applied only at the encoder side or via simple feature pooling and therefore do not fully exploit complementary decoding paths for both fine (local) and coarse (global) cues. Prior work has limited explicit modeling of inter-annotator/view variance and rarely leverages frequency-domain transformations to simulate annotation-style variability. Boundary precision is often addressed by post-processing or auxiliary losses, but integrated segmentation–regression (signed distance) consistency has not been widely combined with temporally-accumulated confidence weighting. Abstract: We propose a structured research pipeline to evaluate SASNet, a semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation framework that addresses limited annotations, annotation variance, and boundary precision. SASNet uses a shared encoder and two decoders specialized for low-level (fine-detail) and high-level (context) features. During training we apply a Scale-Aware Adaptive Reweight (SAR) mechanism that temporally accumulates per-voxel confidence across epochs to form pixel-wise ensemble weights for combining branch predictions. To simulate annotation variability we apply a view-variance augmentation pipeline in the 3D Fourier domain (rotation in frequency space followed by inverse transform) to generate diverse input views. The ensembled segmentation is converted to a signed distance map (SDM) and used to impose segmentation–regression consistency on both decoders. The pipeline evaluates performance on LA, Pancreas-CT, and BraTS with 10% and 20% labeled fractions, measuring voxel overlap and boundary metrics. We expect SASNet to provide improved Dice and boundary distances compared with existing semi-supervised baselines while approaching fully supervised performance. Experiments: Datasets and splits: LA (100 volumes): use same preprocessing as prior work; training set = 80 volumes, validation = 20; for semi-supervised experiments randomly designate 10% (8) or 20% (16) of training volumes as labeled and treat the remaining training volumes as unlabeled. Pancreas-CT (82 volumes): training 62, validation 20; labeled fractions 10% (6) and 20% (12). BraTS (335 cases): training 250, validation 25, test 60; labeled fractions 10% (25) and 20% (50) drawn from training set. Baselines: fully-supervised VNet (backbone), and semi-supervised baselines implemented with the same backbone and training recipe: Mean-Teacher style consistency, uncertainty-weighted pseudo-labeling, dual-task/pyramid-consistency method, multi-scale encoder fusion, and a representative mutual-consistency pseudo-label method. Evaluation metrics: Dice, Jaccard, HD95 (95% Hausdorff), ASD; report mean ± standard deviation over 5 independent random labeled/unlabeled splits and 5 training seeds. Training protocol: VNet backbone, shared encoder, dual decoders; SGD with momentum 0.9, initial LR=0.01, batch size 4, random crop sizes per dataset (LA 112×112×80, Pancreas-CT 96×96×96, BraTS 96×96×96), total epochs 200, consistency coefficient gamma ramped to final value over first 40 epochs (sigmoid ramp-up), sharpening temperature 0.1, SAR accumulates confidence from previous two epochs with residual coefficient alpha=0.5. Ablation studies: (A) SAR on vs off (temporal confidence weighting replaced by simple average); (B) view-variance augmentation on vs off (no FT-domain rotations); (C) SDM-based regression consistency vs direct cross-entropy on ensembled predictions; (D) one-branch (high-level only) vs two-branch (low+high) decoders; (E) low-level decoder depth: 3-layer vs 4-layer. Additional analyses: sensitivity sweep of hyperparameters beta (segmentation weight) ∈ {0.5,1.0} and gamma end value ∈ {0.5,1.0} with/without ramp-up; compute parameters, FLOPs, and GPU inference time on NVIDIA A100. Statistical testing: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing SASNet to best baseline across validation folds; significance threshold p<0.05. Success criteria: SASNet shows statistically significant improvements in mean Dice and HD95 over baselines for both 10% and 20% labeled settings across at least two datasets. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Pseudo-label bias and confirmation: SAR relies on temporal accumulation of predictions; persistent systematic errors in both branches can reinforce incorrect labels across epochs. 2) View-variance realism: frequency-domain rotations may produce image variations that do not reflect actual annotator variability or plausible anatomy, potentially hurting generalization. 3) Computational cost: dual-decoder architecture and temporal accumulation increase parameter count, memory footprint, and inference latency compared with single-branch networks, limiting deployment on resource-constrained systems. 4) Dataset bias and scope: evaluation limited to LA, Pancreas-CT, and BraTS; results may not generalize to other organs, modalities, slice-based 2D pipelines, or multi-center heterogenous scanners. 5) Sensitivity to hyperparameters: SAR alpha, ramp-up schedule, SDM normalization, and decoder depth may require dataset-specific tuning; unstable settings can degrade performance. 6) Boundary supervision mismatch: conversion of probabilistic ensembles to SDM assumes crisp GT boundaries; for highly ambiguous labels or multi-rater GT, SDM targets may be noisy. 7) Statistical variability: limited labeled fractions and small labeled sample sizes increase variance of reported metrics and require multiple seeds/splits for robust conclusions.
